parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: As a fleet technician, I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, set up our charging pads at our sites, and send drones to charge. I also take drones out of service for repairs and put them back when they are ready.
The question: What do you record about a drone when you add it to the fleet?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you take a drone out of service for repair while it is already planned for a flight, what should happen to that flight?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When you send a drone to charge, how do you choose the charging pad, and what must the service stop you from doing?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Is there anything about your drones, charging pads or repairs that people outside your company must never see?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What is your biggest worry about how the new service could make your job harder or cause harm?

Q7
The answer just before it: I worry about the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment because they are unreliable. An instruction might get through twice, and as the sender, I often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.
The question: Besides unreliable instruction links, what else worries you or has gone wrong in the past?

Q8
The answer just before it: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, which causes reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned.
The question: Is there anything further that worries you, beyond links, radio coverage, drones restarting in flight and batteries draining faster?

Q9
The answer just before it: I worry about the single server running the service, which is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes while our company accepts a few minutes of interruption.
The question: Any other concerns or past problems you have not yet mentioned?

Q10
The answer just before it: I worry about the service being updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and that it occasionally crashes. We accept a few minutes of interruption, but I know regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: Beyond regulators asking how drones have been looked after, is there any other concern or fact I should know?

Q11
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When regulators ask how your drones have been looked after, what do you need to be able to show them?

Q12
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Do your sites and charging pads belong only to your company, or are any shared with other customer companies?

Q13
The answer just before it: Our company has its own charging pads at our own sites, and pads are never lent to another company.
The question: What can a charging pad do and not do, for example how many drones can it charge at once and can every drone use every pad?

Q14
The answer just before it: Each company has several connector types in use, and they are not interchangeable. Because our drones are of several models from different manufacturers, they use different charging connectors. I don't know how many drones a pad can charge at once.
The question: How do your drone models differ from each other in ways that matter for which jobs they can fly?

Q15
The answer just before it: Our drones differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, and which sensors they carry, such as cameras, thermal cameras, and laser scanners. These differences matter because deliveries carry a load from one site to another, while inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started.
The question: What happens to a drone when you retire it, and can a retired drone ever come back or have its records removed?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: When a drone is taken out of service for repairs, what is it not allowed to do until you put it back?

Q17
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Can a drone that is charging, or one that is low on battery, be given a flight, and who decides?

Q18
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Do you and the dispatchers ever get in each other's way over the same drone, and what happens then?

Q19
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What instructions do you give to drones and charging equipment through the links, and what goes wrong when one gets through twice?

Q20
The answer just before it: I don't know what specific instructions I give through the links. I do know that an instruction may get through twice, and as the sender, I often cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.
The question: Can a drone fly farther than one full battery by stopping to recharge at pads on the way, and does the pad need the right connector for that drone?
